title: Angle Sums of Polygons

findings.finding: The topic has no opening review of substitution and bracket evaluation, both used directly in the heptagon example.
findings.breakdown: Following S=180(n−2) through 180(7−2) requires replacing the variable and evaluating the bracket before multiplying.
findings.checked: The investigation develops the geometric pattern but does not rehearse substitution into an algebraic expression. There is no preceding topic in the supplied booklet.
findings.assumptions: Substitution and order of operations are prior learning. The finding concerns those decisions, not multiplication that a calculator could perform.

repair.proposal: Before p3-investigation, add: (a) Evaluate 12(7−2). (b) P=4s. Find P when s=6. (c) T=5(k−3). Find T when k=9. Answers: 60, 24, 30. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse substitution and bracket evaluation before using the polygon formula.

findings.finding: Parts 7a and 7f repeat the same complete side-count task with an interior angle sum of 1260°.
findings.breakdown: The shared instruction, given angle sum and requested quantity are unchanged, with no stated retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: Compared both complete parts under p6-q7-root. The replacement gives 1980÷180+2=13 sides.
findings.doneWhen: The later copy uses a different angle sum while retaining the task structure.

findings.finding: Extend Question 8 by comparing its regular polygon with one having twice as many sides.
findings.breakdown: The comparison connects the total interior angle sum with the size of each interior angle.
findings.checked: The original polygon has 16 sides and interior angles of 157.5°. A 32-sided polygon has total 5400° and individual angles 168.75°, an increase of 11.25°. These repeat the calculations already required by Question 8.
findings.assumptions: The missing regular-polygon method identified in c5 is supplied before Question 8.

repair.proposal: After p6-q8b-node, add optional parts: (c) A second regular polygon has twice as many sides as this polygon. Find its interior angle sum. [5400°] (d) Find each interior angle of the second polygon. [168.75°] (e) By how many degrees has each interior angle increased? [11.25°]

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing polygon and separates each calculation into its own part.

findings.finding: Finding an individual interior angle of a regular polygon is required without teaching equal interior angles and division of the total by the number of sides.
findings.breakdown: The first supplied occurrence is p6-q8b-node: finding the total and side count does not explain why that total can be shared equally. The same missing method affects the later regular-polygon problems.
findings.checked: Searched all supplied teaching. It establishes interior angle totals, missing-angle equations and, later, a separate exterior-angle formula. None teaches individual regular-polygon interior angles before these tasks. The earlier Question 8 requests the method but supplies no instruction.
findings.assumptions: Regular-polygon interior-angle calculation is part of this booklet's polygon content; ordinary division is prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: Before p6-q8-root, add: 'A regular polygon has equal sides and equal interior angles. Divide its interior angle sum by its number of sides. For a regular hexagon, the total is 180(6−2)=720°, so each interior angle is 720°÷6=120°.'

findings.doneWhen: The equal-angle reason and division method are taught before their first required use.

findings.finding: Vary the number of equal unknown angles sharing a fixed remaining angle total.
findings.breakdown: The sequence makes students distinguish the remaining total of 240° from the size of each equal unknown angle.
findings.checked: A pentagon's total is 540°, leaving 240° after the known angles. Sharing it between one, two and three unknown angles gives 240°, 120° and 80°. The first pentagon is concave, which p8-guided-b already introduces. The unpatterned hexagon gives (720−450)÷2=135°.
findings.assumptions: Text descriptions may be inserted as additional parts of Question 2.

repair.proposal: Insert after p9-q2b, renumbering the existing later parts. Add only this instruction: 'Predict how each equal unknown angle changes.' (c) A pentagon has four known interior angles totalling 300° and one remaining angle x°. Find x. [240°] (d) A pentagon has three known interior angles totalling 300° and two remaining angles each x°. Find x. [120°] (e) A pentagon has two known interior angles totalling 300° and three remaining angles each x°. Find x. [80°] Follow with (f) A hexagon has four known interior angles totalling 450° and two remaining angles each x°. Find x. [135°] The pentagon total and known-angle total stay fixed; the number of equal unknown angles varies.

findings.doneWhen: The three-part run and unpatterned follow-up appear together with only one added prediction instruction.

findings.finding: The inverse exterior-angle example uses an equation with an unknown denominator without an opening review of that algebra.
findings.breakdown: The step from 12=360/n to n=360/12 requires multiplying by the unknown and then dividing by the known coefficient. Earlier additive and linear equations do not rehearse this form.
findings.checked: No review occurs in this topic. Earlier practice includes inverse interior-angle calculations and linear equations, but no unknown-denominator equation. The topic's investigation does not supply that algebraic preparation.
findings.assumptions: Unknown-denominator equations are prior learning from the separate equations or rearranging-formulas teaching. Calculator availability does not remove the rearrangement decision.

repair.proposal: At the topic opening, add: Solve (a) 8n=360; (b) 12=360/n; (c) 20=360/n. Answers: n=45, n=30, n=18. In checking the review, connect multiplying by n with dividing by the known coefficient.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse the denominator form before p16-sides-example.

findings.finding: p17-q4-a repeats the complete 15° exterior-angle task from p16-guided-c.
findings.breakdown: The given exterior angle, regularity condition and requested side count are unchanged, with no explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: Compared the full prompts. The proposed replacement gives 360÷40=9 sides.
findings.assumptions: Guided practice followed by independent practice does not itself state a purpose for repeating an unchanged whole task.

repair.proposal: Change p17-q4-a to: 'Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 40°. Find the number of sides of the polygon.' Answer: 9 sides.

findings.doneWhen: The later task retains its structure with different numerical givens.

findings.finding: Extend the octagon question by comparing it with a regular polygon having twice as many sides.
findings.breakdown: The comparison connects a halved exterior angle with the corresponding increase in the interior angle.
findings.checked: For 16 sides, the exterior angle is 360÷16=22.5° and the interior angle is 157.5°. This is 22.5° larger than the octagon's 135°. Both methods are explicitly taught by this topic.
findings.assumptions: The additional parts are optional follow-up work.

repair.proposal: After p18-q8-c, add: (d) Find each exterior angle of a regular 16-sided polygon. [22.5°] (e) Find each interior angle of that polygon. [157.5°] (f) How much larger is this interior angle than the octagon's interior angle? [22.5°]

findings.doneWhen: The numerical comparison follows the existing octagon question as separate parts.

protectedGroups.observation: Each additional side produces one additional triangle, leading to n-2 triangles.
protectedGroups.varies: The number of sides increases, then becomes symbolic; supplied diagonals give way to student completion.
protectedGroups.invariant: Triangles partition the polygon from one vertex, and each contributes 180°.

protectedGroups.observation: Finding each regular polygon angle requires equal sharing whether the total is supplied or calculated.
protectedGroups.varies: The total changes from given information to a quantity students must calculate.
protectedGroups.invariant: Divide the interior angle sum by the number of sides.

protectedGroups.observation: Different numbers of supplementary pairs and different interior totals leave the exterior total unchanged.
protectedGroups.varies: Number of vertices, combined angle total and interior-angle total.
protectedGroups.invariant: Each interior–exterior pair totals 180° and the exterior total is 360°.

protectedGroups.observation: Increasing the common exterior angle reduces the number of sides when the exceptional-angle structure stays fixed.
protectedGroups.varies: The common angle changes from 15° to 20°.
protectedGroups.invariant: Two exterior angles are twice the others and all exterior angles total 360°.

protectedGroups.observation: The same interior-angle-sum method gives either an ordinary or a reflex missing interior angle.
protectedGroups.varies: Convex versus concave polygon and the unknown angle's size.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing one polygon changes the gap at the shared vertex.
protectedGroups.varies: A square becomes a regular pentagon.
protectedGroups.invariant: The regular hexagon and full-turn equation.

protectedGroups.observation: The supplied relationship determines how many copies of z make 180°.

sequences.title: Problems involving angle sum of a polygon
Exterior angle sum of a polygon

dropped.reason: The immediately preceding topic's practice already requires solving for an unknown: p6-q7-root finds n from interior angle totals, and p6-q8a-node repeats that inverse calculation. This defeats the opening-review claim under the explicit exemption for skills practised in the preceding topic or exercise. Coefficient division in later tasks is also not a step of the targeted worked example.

candidates.finding: The example depends on solving a linear equation, but the topic has no opening review to check that prerequisite.

dropped.reason: This is a closing challenge using prior triangle and congruence reasoning, rather than requiring a separately taught central-angle formula. Joining the centre to all vertices forms congruent triangles by SSS: polygon sides are equal and radii are equal. Their equal central angles share 360°, giving 45° and then the required reflex angle of 315°. Congruence is taught separately in the listed course library, and p11-q6-root already requires triangle reasoning within a regular polygon.

candidates.finding: The regular-octagon question introduces central angles without teaching why adjacent radii divide the full turn equally.

dropped.reason: The complete parent question supplies an explicit comparison purpose: p17-q5-c asks what happens to exterior-angle size as the side count increases. The pentagon, heptagon and 30-sided polygon in p17-q5-b provide the values for that comparison, following the explanatory hexagon part. This defeats the claim of repetition without an instructional purpose.

candidates.finding: p17-q5-b-i repeats the complete regular-pentagon exterior-angle calculation from p17-q3-a.
